Physiological mechanisms:  
How is blood flow  regulated in response to change in 
temperature?
Cutaneous vascular tone regulated by:
•   Systemic  Neural mechanisms
•    Local mechanisms

Tonic Sympathetic Vasoconstrictor system 
Norepinephrine released from sympathetic nerve endings
Bind to α1 adrenoceptors 
Systemic & Cutaneous vasoconstriction
Sympathetic Cholinergic Vasodilator system
• Becomes active only when core body temperature rises
• Increases skin blood flow and sweating
            
Systemic mechanisms
Peripheral and hypothalamic thermoreceptors

Immersing hand in cold water (5-6oC)
A) Systemic effect –
     Peripheral and hypothalamic thermoreceptors 
Homeostatic feedback mechanism 
     Increase in tonic sympathetic vasoconstrictor activity: 
          ↑ norepinephrine released
    Release of adrenaline from adrenal gland
     α1 adrenoceptors – Constriction of arterioles, increased TPR & hence BP
          
B) Local effects –
   1. Upregulation of cutaneous  α2C receptors
        Increased sensitivity to noradrenaline on postsynaptic α2C  receptors
   2. Inhibition of Nitric Oxide (NO) release & activity 
Baroreceptor reflex: Increased blood pressure activates baroreceptors  → Stimulates 
the vagus nerve → Reflex reduction in heart rate (bradycardia) may follow in some 
subjects.

Other possible mechanisms of vasoconstriction:
Adrenaline from the adrenal gland: amplifying vasoconstriction throughout 
the body
Cummings M etal., The role of adrenal medullary catecholamine release in the response to a 
cold pressor test. Cardiovasc Res. . 1983 Apr;17(4):189-91.
Endothelin-1 Production: The cold stimulus increases endothelin-1, a 
potent vasoconstrictor produced by endothelial cells. promoting 
vasoconstriction.
(F Fyhrquist et al., Raised plasma endothelin-I concentration following cold pressor test. 
Biochem Biophys Res Commun. . 1990 May 31;169(1):217-21).
Angiotensin II: a potent vasoconstrictor, can contribute to the 
vasoconstriction
Israel A etal., Effect of AT 1 Angiotensin II Receptor Antagonistson the Sympathetic Response to 
a Cold Pressor Testin Healthy Volunteers. American Journal of Therapeutics 14, 183–188 (2007)

Net Result in cold water:
    Vasoconstriction →  ↓ blood flow
    Vasoconstriction →  ↑ BP
                          
An increase in BP reflects a decrease in blood flow
Conserves heat
Pain and stress response:
Cold stress also stimulates the release of cortisol and endogenous opioids 
like β-endorphins to modulate the pain response

Experiment 2: 
Effect of Ischaemia on Peripheral Circulation.
Apparatus: 
Inflatable sphygmomanometer cuff, electronic blood pressure monitor, 
stopwatch
Aim: to investigate changes to blood pressure (and by inference 
blood flow) during recovery from short period of ischaemia to the 
forearm/hand
Reactive hyperaemia

Experimental Procedure:
1.
Measure baseline BP using electronic BP monitor. (mean of 2 recordings of SBP & DBP)
2.  Wrap the manual cuff on the other arm inflate to 20mm Hg above the measured systolic BP to cause 
occlusion of blood flow to forearm/hand  (do NOT inflate above 160 mmHg)
Keep cuff inflated for 30secs-1 minute ONLY 
(If at any time you feel pain, discomfort, numbness or tingling remove the cuff immediately)
3. After 1 minute remove the manual cuff and immediately measure blood pressure on the other arm 
with the electronic monitor
4. Continue to measure BP at 30 second intervals for 3 minute

Immersion of hand in 
cold water (4-60C)
•
Risks are minimal at short duration of 1.5 minutes.
•
Only very occasionally, cold burns / frostnip / frostbite if exposed for long 
duration.
•
Pain/discomfort
•
Numbness & reduced dexterity if exposed to longer duration
•
Exacerbation of medical conditions (eg Raynaud’s)
Hand immersion hot 
water (45-460C)

Risks are unlikely at this temperature and short duration, but possible 
redness, pain, discomfort.
•

error

Aggravation of skin conditions (eczema, dermatitis) with longer exposure 
•
Circulatory or neurological reaction (e.g. Light headedness dizziness,
